title: What science can't say
hookLine: whether life has meaning, what is sacred: questions for the traditions and for you

lines: NOT ONE MY INSTRUMENTS CAN ANSWER.
cards: Try a different kind of question on a scientist. Not does meditation lower stress, but should I forgive my father? Not does awe make people kinder, but is anything sacred?
Not how long do people with friends live, but what is a life for? A good scientist will usually pause, then say something like: that's a real question. It's just not one my instruments can answer.
For three weeks this path has been in the lab: six breaths a minute, sixty-six days, trees, sleep, sugar pills. Useful, and honest about its limits.

teach.h: SCIENCE ASKS WHAT IS, AND HOW MUCH.
teach.b: Science does its part beautifully. It asks what is, and how, and how much. It measures, compares, tests, and changes its mind when the evidence changes.
The word comes from the Latin scientia, knowledge, and it has kept this path honest for weeks. Then there's the gap.
In the 1700s the Scottish philosopher David Hume noticed writers sliding from is to ought. They'd describe how things are, then, without saying how they got there, tell you how things should be.

Hume said that step needs explaining. Science can tell you that social ties are linked to longer life. It can't, by itself, tell you that a longer life is what matters most, or that you owe your friends your time.
Those are questions of value. Now, without ranking anyone: the traditions each find meaning and the sacred somewhere the instruments don't reach: in God, in the dharma, in the way.
Some believers say science and faith simply answer different questions.

teach.h: FAITH, GOULD, THE CRITICS, THE CHOOSERS.
teach.b: The paleontologist Stephen Jay Gould argued something similar from outside any faith: two domains, facts and values, each with its own teachers.
Other thinkers disagree, and expect science to explain a great deal more about morality and meaning over time.

teach.h: WHAT HELPS, AND WHAT IT'S FOR.
teach.b: Some existentialist philosophers say meaning isn't found in the world at all; it's made by what you choose.
And Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote that even if every possible scientific question were answered, the problems of life would not yet have been touched.
The traditions you visited this year, and your own reflection, live in that space. The lab can tell you what helps. Only you, and the traditions you listen to, can tell you what it's for.

how: People on their own path often use research to choose practices that help, and turn to philosophy, religious traditions, conversation and reflection for questions of meaning and value.

o: a philosopher who said is doesn't give you ought
a preacher who said faith and science never meet
a scientist who said facts alone can tell right

games.q: beyond the lab — tap the pairs.

s: science can tell you whether you should forgive someone
it can study forgiveness; whether you should is a question of value.
Hume noticed writers sliding from how things are to how they should be
he said the step from is to ought needs explaining.
everyone agrees science and faith answer different questions
some say so; others expect science to explain much more over time.

games.q: a study shows people with friends live longer. does that tell you what matters most in life?
o: yes: longer life is the goal, science says so.
no: it tells you what is; what matters is a question of value.
games.why: science shows the link. whether a longer life matters most, or why friends matter, is for you and the traditions.

practice: Write down one question that matters to you and that no experiment could answer: what do I owe my parents, is there anything after this, what would a good life look like for me?
Don't answer it; just write it as honestly as you can. Then sit with it, the way you'd sit with a friend who asked it.

wordCard.voice: Hume, who noticed writers sliding from is to ought: science tells us what is, but meaning, value and the sacred live beyond the lab. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: knowledge, from scire, to know; the root of science.

carryVoice: Your line: beyond the lab. Some questions were never the lab's to answer. That's day three hundred twenty-three.

sources.work: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40)
